newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Dutch present first EU farm price compromise.
newsitem.headline: Dutch present first EU farm price compromise.

text.p: Dutch Agriculture Minister Jozias Van Aartsen on Tuesday presented a compromise EU farm price package for next year, keeping a controversial proposal to slash aid to wheat farmers.

The 3-1/2 page text, presented on the second day of the annual EU farm price marathon, also contained "sweeteners" on sugar and other farm products demanded by ministers and called for a five percent cereals set-aside rate in 1998.
Set-aside is a scheme intended to remove costly grain mountains, under which farmers must take a certain percentage of their land out of production to obtain EU subsidies.
EU officials said the initial Dutch compromise would almost certainly be rejected by ministers and the EU's farm chief Franz Fischler when discussed later on Tuesday.

"It's part of the ritual," said one official, explaining that the Dutch EU Presidency would have to draft at least one A Commission spokesman said that the Dutch compromise was unacceptable on two points -- set-aside and sugar storage refunds.
"We need all the (crop) data before we can fix the set-aside rate," spokesman Gerard Kiely told reporters, adding that the Commission could not be bound to five percent so early.
On sugar, the Commission says that the Dutch proposal would cost too much and did not reflect lower storage costs following a fall in interest rates.
Earlier, French Farm Minister Louis Le Pensec told journalists: "Seeking a solution will not be easy. We are still a long way from agreement."

Ministers will insist that the cereals aid cut should be shelved. On Monday, a large majority attacked a proposal to cut payments to cereals farmers by 1.4 billion ecus ($1.6 billion) to help fund aid for beef producers hit by the mad cow crisis.

They disputed a claim by EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler that cereals farmers were over-compensated for cuts in support prices and said there was enough spare cash in the 1997 farm budget to help the beef farmers.

Fischler insisted the aid could be adjusted to match price changes and added that there was no room in the 1998 budget to compensate farmers after a fall in prices due to the health scare over bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
Fischler said he was disappointed with ministers' expensive "wish lists" which complicated what was an otherwise straightforward package of mainly unchanged prices.
Britain was one of the few countries to support Fischler's bid to reduce cereals aid.
"The farm price package must stay within the budget," British Farm Minister Jack Cunningham told reporters.
